Approval & Spend Guardrails ​

Saidi's guardrails are layered so that no single mistake — a bad plan, a runaway loop, a too-permissive agent — can turn into an expensive one.

Layer 1: the approval gate ​

Set per project, in memory/projects/<name>.md:

markdown
---
branch: new
approval: confirm
verify: npm run build && npm test
---
  • approval: confirm parks every write as a structured PendingApproval.
  • branch: new means work lands on a saidi/* branch with a PR — never on your checked-out branch, and never merged for you.
  • verify: runs after the commit and reports pass/fail mechanically.

Unset or invalid values fall back to the safe policy (new + confirm). Change the operator-wide fallback in Settings → System if you need a different default, but raise it deliberately — this is the one dial that decides whether a model can write to your repo unattended.

Layer 2: auto-approve, scoped ​

Rather than switching a whole project to approval: auto, Settings exposes per-action auto-approval (AutoApproveAction). Grant the specific low-risk actions you are tired of clicking, and leave the rest gated. The narrower grant is almost always the right one.

Layer 3: agent permissions ​

An agent's permission (all / read-only / custom) is enforced by handing the SDK a restricted tool set with a canUseTool gate behind it. A read-only agent cannot write even inside a work delegation — the narrower of the two always wins.

For anything touching an external system, prefer custom with a short explicit tools: list over all.

Layer 4: spend ​

Enforcement runs before a delegation is dispatched. It can:

  • Block the call when the operator's allowance is exhausted (usageBlockReason).
  • Clamp the effort tier down instead of refusing, so a run degrades rather than dying (clampEffort).
  • Deny agent access or a specific run action on a permission check.

Everything spent is recorded per call in the run's usageLog, with unpriced flagged rather than silently counted as zero — a cap you cannot measure is not a cap.

Layer 5: attempt budgets ​

  • A global attempt ceiling applies to every task.
  • A per-task attemptBudget can lower it — and cannot exceed the global. A one-shot inbox lookup and a twenty-minute document rebuild should not get the same number of retries.
  • failureKind routes the retry: environment_failure and semantic_failure do not deserve the same response, and treating every rejection as "redo the whole task" is how a budget disappears.

Layer 6: concurrency locks ​

A repo lock serialises delegations against one checkout; custom agents take an equivalent agent lock. Two runs cannot interleave commits on the same working directory. Custom agents also get a per-run workDir, so concurrent runs never share a directory.

Layer 7: reflex controls ​

For anything event-triggered, see Building a Reflex:

cooldownSec, dedupKey, maxFires, requireApproval, enabled, plus a bus-level chain-depth cap on emitEvent chains.

A sane starting posture ​

SettingStart at
Project approvalconfirm
Project branchnew
Project verifyYour test command — always set this
New custom agent permissionread-only, widen only on evidence
Reflexes that writerequireApproval: true + a dedupKey + maxFires
Execution mode for repeatable workguided

Relax individual dials once you have watched them hold. Relax them one at a time, so you know which one was load-bearing.

See also: Modes & Permissions · Project Policy
